newsitem.title: USA: U.S. author who killed himself faced investigation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. author who killed himself faced investigation.

text.p: Michael Dorris, the author of a prize-winning book on raising a brain-damaged son, was under investigation for child sexual abuse in the months before his suicide last week, friends said on Tuesday.
Minneapolis police confirmed that Dorris, 52, was the subject of a criminal investigation and said a public statement would be made next week once the case was formally closed because of his death.

Sources familiar with the case told Reuters the charges involved child sexual abuse and friends said the allegations arose out of the bitter divorce and child custody proceedings he was involved in with his wife, novelist Louise Erdrich. The sources declined to go into detail and friends called the allegations inconceivable.
"On the basis of a long and close relationship with Michael Dorris I regard the charges as utterly implausible," Dorris's agent Charles Rembar said.

Douglas Kelley, the lawyer helping Dorris in the Minneapolis abuse investigation, said, "To speculate on any possible wrongdoing by Mr. Dorris is cruel and inappropriate, bringing only added sorrow to a family that has suffered a terrible loss."
He said the writer was never charged with anything and had he been, "he would never have been convicted of any crime."
Dorris and Erdrich were a celebrated team who often edited each other's works and dedicated their books to each other.

Once regarded as the "the literary couple of the 1980s," they had been separated for two years with friends saying that the split turned bitter in recent months as discussions of custody of their three young children began.

Dorris was found on the floor of a Concord, New Hampshire, motel room last Friday. Police said he died after ingesting 2-1/2 bottles of pills and fastening a plastic bag over his head with an elastic cord to keep it in place.
Police ruled the death a suicide, saying he left a note apologising to the person who discovered his body for any shock that might ensue and saying goodbye to his friends.

His body was found on the day he was to have been honoured by Dartmouth College for having founded its Native American Studies Programme. He had told Darmouth in advance that he would not be able to attend because of illness.

Dorris, an essayist, children's writer and novelist, was the author of "The Broken Cord," which won the 1989 National Book Critics Circle Award for its powerful account of raising an adopted Indian boy damaged by foetal alcohol syndrome.
The bestseller drew international attention to the harm caused by women drinking during pregnancy and led to laws requiring bars and liquor stores to display warnings.
The news of Dorris' death sent shockwaves through the literary community. They were equally stunned by the news about the possible criminal charges.

"I can tell you that had the charges been aired, Michael would have been cleared. This is a tragic story. It is unthinkable that he is not with us and unthinkable that he is being killed twice (by the allegations)," said former Detroit News book editor Ruth Coughlin, a close friend.
She said the last weeks of Dorris's life were an agony. "I never heard heard a man in in greater despair," she said, recounting how she and other friends tried to help him.
Dorris attempted suicide in March and was committed to a hospital for a brief time. But he left the hospital and was reported as a missing person.

Erdrich told the Minneapolis Star Tribune Dorris "did a lot for the world" but was subject to powerful depressions. "Even the wisest and most self-aware people can be caught off guard," she said, declining to discuss the sex abuse charges.
Dorris, of mixed Irish, French and American Indian ancestry, was raised in part on a reservation in Montana.

He was the first unmarried American male to legally adopt a child. His son Abel died at age 23 in a car accident in 1992. Dorris also adopted two other Native American children who suffered from a lesser form of foetal alcohol syndrome.
